conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode. Helpers: range(n) = high[n]-low[n]; body(n) = close[n]-open[n]; avgRange(N) = average of range over the N bars ending at bar 1; tick = instrument minimum price move (structural constant); highest(x,N)[k] / lowest(x,N)[k] = extreme over N bars ending at bar k. Pages 80 and 84 of this file lost inter-word spaces during extraction; content there was read and mined normally.

candidates.name: BullTrendBar
candidates.quote: Is that bar a trend bar, opening near one end and closing near the other, or is it a trading range bar with a small body and one or two large tails?
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 0 is a bull trend bar, opening near its low and closing near its high, with a body that is most of the bar's range.
notes: Brooks gives no number; this and the corpus's TrendBarBodyFraction/BullTrendBar rules are the same idea, redefined here as the book's earliest use of the concept.

candidates.name: DojiBar
candidates.quote: Is that bar a trend bar, opening near one end and closing near the other, or is it a trading range bar with a small body and one or two large tails?
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 0 is a trading-range (doji) bar, the opposite of a trend bar -- a small body relative to its range, with one or two large tails.
notes: Direction-agnostic; whether the doji leans bull or bear is a separate close-position test, not part of this primitive.

candidates.name: BreakoutHigherHighLowConfirmation
candidates.quote: if the market goes above a significant prior high and each subsequent bar forms a low that is above the prior bar's low and a high that is above the prior bar's high, then this price action indicates that the market will likely be higher on some subsequent bar
candidates.description: Context filter: after a breakout above a prior significant high, each of the last N bars made both a higher high and a higher low than the bar before it -- confirms the breakout and favors with-trend entries.
candidates.pseudocode: for k in 0..confirmBars-1: high[k] > high[k+1] && low[k] > low[k+1]

complexity.reason: small window loop of fixed-offset comparisons

notes: Brooks does not give a bar count for 'each subsequent bar'; confirmBars is a reading of the passage.

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutSmallInsideBarReversal
candidates.quote: if the market breaks out to the upside and then the next bar is a small inside bar (its high is not higher than that of the large breakout bar) and then the following bar has a low that is below this small bar, the odds of a failed breakout and a reversal back down increase considerably
candidates.description: Long side (mirror of the book's bear example): a bear breakout bar is followed by a small inside bar (its low not below the breakout bar's low), then this bar closes above that small bar's high -- fade the failed breakout upward.
candidates.pseudocode: close[2] < open[2] && body(2) >= bodyFraction * range(2) && low[1] >= low[2] && range(1) <= smallFraction * range(2) && close[0] > high[1]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the small inside bar's high (book's mirror: sell stop below it)
notes: Book's own example is a bull breakout failing to the downside; mirrored here per the long-side convention.

candidates.name: Leg
candidates.quote: bar 3 was the first leg down after the strong move up to bar 2. That made it the A leg of the ABC pullback. The little move up to the bar 4 high was the B leg, and the move down to the bar 5 low was the C leg.
candidates.description: Primitive: a leg is one directional swing between two pivots (a run of bars making new extremes in one direction, ended by a bar that fails to extend it). Legs are counted to label ABC pullbacks and high 1/high 2/high 3/... or low 1/low 2/... entries.
candidates.pseudocode: swingPivotDetection(); legCount = number of alternating directional swings since the last trend extreme

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and leg counting over a variable-length window; the definition of when a leg ends is itself a design decision

notes: Foundational primitive for H1/H2/L1/L2 and ABC patterns throughout the trilogy.

candidates.name: HighNPullbackEntry
candidates.quote: when there is a pullback in a bull leg... then the first bar that goes above the high of the prior bar is a high 1 long entry... If the pullback continues down for a second leg... the first bar after bar 5 that goes above the high of the prior bar would be a high 2 entry.
candidates.description: In a bull trend, after exactly N pullback legs down, the first bar that closes above the prior bar's high is a high-N long entry (high 1, high 2, high 3, ...). Mirror: low-N short entries in a bear trend.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the prior bar's high (short: sell stop one tick below the prior bar's low)

complexity.reason: requires leg counting via swing-pivot detection (see Leg)

notes: The book's H1/H2/L1/L2 counting setups, generalized to a single parameterized rule by leg number; H3/H4 are the same rule at pullbackLegNumber 3/4.

candidates.name: FailedHighNReversal
candidates.quote: If the market then trades below the low of the two-legged pullback, everyone will assume that the market will likely have at least one more leg down.
candidates.description: After a high-N long entry, the market instead trades below the low of the pullback that produced it (the ABC low): treat this as a failed high-N and a signal that at least one more down leg follows -- a short entry on the breakout of that pullback low.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the pullback's low

complexity.reason: needs the same leg/pivot state as HighNPullbackEntry plus tracking of the specific pullback's extreme

notes: Institutions who bought the failing high-N 'will buy more all the way down to one tick above that key protective stop price' -- a with-trend add, not mined separately (position sizing).

candidates.name: ExtremeConsecutiveTrendBarsFadeContext
candidates.quote: The market can reach extremes in any type of behavior, like the number of consecutive bear trend bars; the number of consecutive days where the range is half of the average or twice the average; and just about anything else that you can imagine.
candidates.description: Context filter: N or more consecutive same-direction trend bars is an extreme state that institutions fade; permits a countertrend (fade) entry only once this extreme count is reached. Brooks's caveat ('unless you are very confident, do not fade the trend') is not separately mechanizable and is left as a confidence note.

complexity.reason: 'extreme' is a design decision -- which measure and threshold count as extreme is not specified by Brooks

notes: Brooks lists several other extreme measures (range vs. average, consecutive higher-highs) as equally valid; this candidate mines only the trend-bar-count version.

candidates.name: BarsSinceEmaTouchExtreme
candidates.quote: if the daily SPY is in a bull channel and it has not touched the moving average for 45 days and it has only done that once in the past 10 years, the current behavior is extremely unusual.
candidates.description: Context filter: the market has gone at least N bars without the price touching its EMA -- an extreme extension that institutions view as due for a pullback to the average.

complexity.reason: needs an EMA plus a persistent bars-since-touch counter

notes: Brooks's example is the daily SPY specifically; the mechanism generalizes to any bar size.

candidates.name: BreakevenStopAfterPartialProfit
candidates.quote: Move your stop to breakeven and then let the remainder run.
candidates.description: After open profit has reached a partial-profit trigger, tighten the stop for the remaining position to breakeven (the entry price): exit if profit gives back all the way to zero.
candidates.book_order_type: move protective stop to entry price once a partial profit target is reached

complexity.reason: position-state read (MaxPositionProfit) gating a zero-profit exit

notes: Equivalent to ProfitProtector with retracement fixed at 1.0 (give back the entire peak); kept separate since Brooks states it as an unconditional breakeven move, not a fractional giveback.

candidates.name: FibonacciRetracementPullbackEntry
candidates.quote: the first pullback in a new trend often retraces about 62 percent of the first leg but not often enough to place a limit order to enter there.
candidates.description: Long side: the first pullback of a new bull leg reaches down to a Fibonacci fraction of that leg's range; buy a bounce there.
candidates.pseudocode: retracementLevel = legHigh - fibFraction * (legHigh - legLow); low[0] <= retracementLevel && close[0] > retracementLevel
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the retracement level (Brooks explicitly says this is usually unwise)

complexity.reason: needs the leg's high/low from swing-pivot detection

notes: Brooks himself is skeptical: 'most are just approximations and most fail'; kept as a candidate because it is a concrete bar-level test, with confidence marked low to reflect his caveat.

candidates.name: RangeContractionExtreme
candidates.quote: if the recent daily range has shrunk to about a third of its long-term average, it cannot last that way for too long.
candidates.description: Context filter: the recent average bar range has contracted to a small fraction of its long-term average -- an extreme low-volatility state expected to resolve into expansion soon.

complexity.reason: classifying 'cannot last' as an actionable extreme needs a design decision, similar to trading-range classification

notes: Mirror image of AtrAboveAverage-style expansion filters already in the catalog; this is the contraction-extreme form Brooks describes for daily SPY.

rejected.quote: institutions do not have secret meetings to vote on what the price should be
rejected.reason: narrative about institutional behavior; no bar-level test

rejected.quote: they will enter only when they feel that the risk of an adverse move is small
It is fairly common to see a pullback that comes down exactly to the low of that entry bar but not one tick lower... there must be institutional size volume protecting the stops
rejected.reason: requires order-book/tick-level data below the bar to detect 'stops not run'

rejected.quote: HFT firms... trading 40 million shares a day on its basket of 4,500 stocks
rejected.reason: descriptive market-structure narrative; no bar-level test

rejected.quote: anything over 100 contracts should be considered institutional in today's Emini market
rejected.reason: needs individual trade size (tick/order-level data), not aggregate bar volume

rejected.quote: it is very common in strong trends for a reversal bar to totally reverse its appearance in the final few seconds before a 5 minute bar closes
rejected.reason: needs intrabar tick data below the bar; the mitigation ('wait for the bar to close') is already the corpus-wide close-based entry convention, not a new rule

rejected.quote: Elliott Wave Theory is also a type of price action analysis, but for most traders it is not tradable
rejected.reason: Brooks himself states it lacks a workable bar-level test ('too much uncertainty')

rejected.quote: Alan Greenspan said that as Fed chairman he was right about 70 percent of the time
Whenever a pundit on television says with certainty that the market is going up...
rejected.reason: narrative about media commentary; no bar-level test

rejected.quote: if a scalper is using a stop that is larger than his profit target, he has to win on 70 percent or more of their trades to be profitable
rejected.reason: general risk/reward arithmetic, not a bar-level entry or exit condition

chapter_summary: Part I's introduction is mostly conceptual: what price action is, why institutions and HFT programs drive it, and why traders should read charts rather than fundamentals or the news. Few of its statements are directly mechanical, but it does establish core primitives reused throughout the trilogy (trend bar vs. doji, the Leg concept behind ABC/H1/H2/L1/L2 counting), a couple of concrete extreme-state fade filters (consecutive trend bars, bars since an EMA touch, range contraction), a breakeven-stop management rule, and a low-confidence Fibonacci retracement entry that Brooks himself is skeptical of. A large fraction of the chapter (HFT mechanics, institutional psychology, media commentary, risk/reward arithmetic) was rejected as narrative or as requiring data below the bar.
